subject: Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)

messages.author: e3daea24651c4835
messages.subject: Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)
parts:
Hi,
I would like to know if some people could successfuly speed up some
steps of the Total Copy Number Analysis, by parallelizing them. Are
there some key time consuming steps that could be easily parallelized
by running concurrent instances of R?
Thanks for your answers,
Nicolas Stransky

messages.author: e3daea24651c4835
messages.subject: Re: Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)
parts:
In particular, if I understand it correctly, the probe-level
summarization for GWS6 is done for each array independently, which
means that in theory, one could launch an R instance for each array
that is being analyzed. I am currently analyzing 96 GWS6 arrays and
the AvgCnPlm step is taking more than 12-13 hours, this is why I would
like to parallelize this step because there are more arrays to come.
Has anyone got hints about how to proceed?

Thank you so much,
Nicolas Stransky

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)
parts: Hi.

On Tue, Apr 8, 2008 at 1:39 PM, Nicolas Stransky
<nicolas....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> In particular, if I understand it correctly, the probe-level
> summarization for GWS6 is done for each array independently, which
> means that in theory, one could launch an R instance for each array
> that is being analyzed. I am currently analyzing 96 GWS6 arrays and
> the AvgCnPlm step is taking more than 12-13 hours, this is why I would
> like to parallelize this step because there are more arrays to come.
> Has anyone got hints about how to proceed?

First, it is often much faster to work toward a local drive than over
a network file system. I say this, because quite a few people are one
a shared file system.

Second, about Avg[Cn]Plm: Yes, the underlying model is a single-array
model. However, due to lack of time, I actually let it inherit from
the ProbelLevelModel class (just like RmaPlm) so that I could reuse
the whole load-fit-save framework. This means it indeed loads data in
chunks of units across all arrays and then fit the data array by
array. It is on my lengthy todo list to make this a truly
array-by-array implementation (the estimates will be the same).

Third, before discussing parallelization, there is one obvious thing
one can do to speed up the processing of chip types with single-probe
probeset. For instance, in GenomeWideSNP_{5|6} all CN units are
single-probe units, but they are still treated as units with unit
groups/probeset in all ways what that means, e.g. loading data in
across arrays wrapped up in a nested list, pass it to the internal fit
function, the unwrap the estimates and store them to file. This is
done although the chip effect estimates for single-probe probesets are
all identical to probe signals (and there is no across-array
parameters/modelling). In other words, one can update the
ProbelLevelModel class, and more specifically the fit() method, to
become aware of single-probe units and just "copy and paste" the probe
signals array by array first. Doing that will probably speed up the
fit() call substantially - probably twice as fast for the GWS5/6
chips. This is on my todo list as well, but since it is a
low-priority for me, it is unlikely that it will make it up to the top
anytime soon. You are more than welcome to contribute to this work.
If you do, please let me know.

Fourth, another thing way down on my todo list is to add a
*bullet-proof* and *cross-platform* file-locking mechanism for writing
to files such that "one" has to wait for the file to be release before
writing to it. Next, fit() of ProbeLevelModel need to be updated to
not process the units chunks in order, but in a random order. With
these two features on can have multiple hosts process the same
PLM/data set at the same time. Again, contributions are most welcome.
The file-locking mechanism is something that should be developed and
tested independently of aroma.affymetrix.

/Henrik

>
> Thank you so much,
>
>
> Nicolas Stransky
> >
>

messages.author: 23d3e7e30355e22d
messages.subject: Re: Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)
parts:
I am also attempting to parallelize total copy number analysis of a
large number of GWS5 chips (~1400). However, a file-locking mechanism
sounds like a difficult and involved approach that could retain some
bottlenecks. A workaround in the interim would be to associate a
unique number with each segment (or "sub-job") of the larger job (most
cluster engines make such a number readily available) and then use
this number to ensure that all files written are unique. A "merging"
phase could follow at the end to combine the results in to a single
result. That may be too much to ask of the ChromosomeExplorer, but at
least the regions.xls file could be reconstituted. This cluster step
is probably only needed for the segmentation step, as this is easily
the most time-consuming.

Henrik, do you have any tips as how one could go about introducing
this extra "cluster node number" parameter and propogating it through
to all files written during the segmentation process? As an
experiment, I naively ran the segmentation on a cluster by breaking up
the chips to be processed over 200 nodes. The nodes all had network
file system access to the results of the previous processing steps.
The analysis was successfully completed, but the nodes overwrote each
other's output files.

Thanks in advance for any suggestions.

John Watkinson

On Tue, Apr 15, 2008 at 8:23 PM, John Watkinson <watk...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am also attempting to parallelize total copy number analysis of a
> large number of GWS5 chips (~1400). However, a file-locking mechanism

> least the regions.xls file could be reconstituted. This cluster step
> is probably only needed for the segmentation step, as this is easily
> the most time-consuming.

I was think of the multi-chip probe summarization methods (PLMs) when
I talked about the file locking mechanism. Those algorithms write to
multiple files multiple times. For the segmentation methods this is
less necessary since they (typically) operate and store data sample by
sample and even chromosome by chromosome. See more comment below.

>
> Henrik, do you have any tips as how one could go about introducing
> this extra "cluster node number" parameter and propogating it through
> to all files written during the segmentation process? As an
> experiment, I naively ran the segmentation on a cluster by breaking up
> the chips to be processed over 200 nodes. The nodes all had network
> file system access to the results of the previous processing steps.
> The analysis was successfully completed, but the nodes overwrote each
> other's output files.

It sounds to me that you are using process() of the ChromsomeExplorer
for executing the segmentation. That is mostly done for your
convenience. However, for distributed processing like what you want,
use fit() of the CopyNumberSegmentationModel, e.g. CbsModel. It
operates on one sample and one chromosome at the time and stores data
by sample and chromosome (stored as binary R files [*.xls]). In that
sense there are no concurrency/dead lock/overwriting issues.

Then, use getRegions() of the same CopyNumberSegmentationModel and the
same sample and chromosome to extract the regions. That call will
call fit() as well, but if/since it is already processed it will just
load the "fit" structure from file. In other words, if all samples
and chromosomes have been processed your "merger" can call
getRegions(..., arrays, chromosomes) to retrieve all identified
regions. You can then also call writeRegions() to write them to file.

To generate the image files in parallel, you can use writeGraphs(...,
arrays, chromosomes).

See process() of ChromosomeExplorer, which is basically a wrapper for
the above, for more details.

Hope this makes it easier for you to do segmentation in parallel.

/Henrik
